column1: RLS security predicates are implemented as {{c1::inline table-valued functions}}.
column2:
An inline table-valued function returns a table from a SELECT expression. RLS uses the presence or absence of a returned row to decide whether the access condition passes. It does not call a function that returns a scalar Boolean.
Review source

column1: An RLS predicate using SELECT 1 WHERE returns {{c1::no rows}} when the access condition is FALSE or UNKNOWN.
column2:
A pattern such as SELECT 1 WHERE condition returns one row only when the condition is TRUE. If it is FALSE or UNKNOWN, it returns an empty table. Returning a row containing 0 is not the same as returning no rows.
Review source

column1: Use WITH {{c1::SCHEMABINDING}} to schema-bind an RLS predicate function.
column2:
WITH SCHEMABINDING ties the function to the definitions of its referenced objects. It prevents incompatible changes to those objects while the dependency exists. The function must be created with this option for use as an RLS predicate.
Review source

column1: RLS {{c1::filter predicates}} silently exclude rows that fail their access condition.
column2:
A filter predicate removes disallowed rows from the operation's accessible set. A SELECT can therefore return fewer rows or an empty result without an error. This differs from a block predicate that rejects a prohibited write.
Review source

column1: SQL Server RLS {{c1::block predicates}} raise an error for prohibited writes.
column2:
A block predicate enforces a condition on a write operation. If that condition fails, SQL Server rejects the operation with an error. It does not silently hide the failed write as a filter hides rows.
Review source

column1: In SQL Server, filter predicates alone do not validate new {{c1::INSERT}} values.
column2:
An INSERT creates a new row instead of reading an existing row through the filter. The insert can succeed even when a later SELECT hides the new row. An AFTER INSERT block predicate can reject such new values.
Review source

column1: In SQL Server, an {{c1::AFTER INSERT}} block predicate validates newly inserted rows.
column2:
AFTER INSERT evaluates the row values produced by the insert. A tenant rule can reject a row whose TenantID does not match the authorized tenant. AFTER describes the values checked, not permission to keep an invalid row.
Review source

column1: In SQL Server, an AFTER UPDATE block predicate checks {{c1::new row values}} when its referenced columns change.
column2:
AFTER UPDATE checks the values after the change, not the original values. It can stop a row from moving into a disallowed tenant. SQL Server skips this predicate if none of its referenced columns change.
Review source

column1: SQL Server uses {{c1::BEFORE DELETE}} as the block-predicate timing for checking rows before deletion.
column2:
BEFORE DELETE checks the existing row before deletion. If the access condition fails, the delete is rejected. There is no new row after deletion for an AFTER DELETE check.
Review source

column1: Set a tenant context with EXEC sys.{{c1::sp_set_session_context}} @key=N'TenantID', @value=42;
column2:
Session context stores named values for the current database connection. The example stores 42 under TenantID so that a predicate can read it. Trusted application code must choose the tenant from authorized identity information.
Review source

column1: Read a session's TenantID value with {{c1::SESSION_CONTEXT}}(N'TenantID').
column2:
SESSION_CONTEXT retrieves a value previously stored under the specified key. The N prefix makes TenantID a Unicode string literal. An RLS predicate can compare the returned tenant value with the row's TenantID.
Review source

column1: SESSION_CONTEXT returns {{c1::sql_variant}} before any explicit conversion to an integer tenant ID.
column2:
sql_variant can hold values of different SQL data types. Casting the session value to int makes the intended tenant-ID type explicit. A value that cannot be converted to int raises a conversion error rather than identifying a valid tenant.
Review source

column1: Set {{c1::@read_only}} = 1 to prevent changing a session-context key again on its logical connection.
column2:
The value cannot be changed again on that logical connection. This protects the value after it is set, but does not make an unauthorized initial value valid. Trusted code must set the correct tenant before locking the key.
Review source

column1: Retrieve the current database user's principal ID with {{c1::DATABASE_PRINCIPAL_ID}}().
column2:
A database principal is a user, role, or similar identity recorded in the database. With no name argument, DATABASE_PRINCIPAL_ID() returns the current user's ID. It does not return an employee number from an application table.
Review source

column1: Test current-user membership in SalesManagers with {{c1::IS_MEMBER}}('SalesManagers') = 1.
column2:
IS_MEMBER checks membership for the current user, not an arbitrary supplied username. A result of 1 means that the user belongs to SalesManagers. An RLS predicate can use this test as one part of its access condition.
Review source

column1: Create the object that binds RLS predicates to tables with {{c1::CREATE SECURITY POLICY}}.
column2:
The function contains the access condition, but a policy attaches that condition to a table. It also selects filter or block behavior and any write-operation timing. Creating the function alone does not protect the table.
Review source

column1: Explicitly enable an RLS policy with WITH (STATE = {{c1::ON}}).
column2:
STATE = ON activates the existing policy and its configured predicates. It does not create new predicate functions or grant SELECT. Users still need the normal permissions for their requested operations.
Review source

column1: Protect both Orders and OrderDetails by adding a predicate binding for {{c1::each table}}.
column2:
A policy binding protects the named table, not every table related to it. Filtering Orders does not automatically protect a direct query against OrderDetails. Add a binding to each table that needs the tenant rule.
Review source

column1: A {{c1::recursive common table expression (CTE)}} can traverse successive employee-to-manager relationships for hierarchy-based row access.
column2:
A recursive CTE starts with an initial set and repeatedly adds related rows. For a management tree, each step can add employees whose manager is already included. This can build the set of owners whose records are accessible.
Review source

column1: An employee hierarchy that starts at the current employee and adds their reports includes {{c1::that employee and all direct and indirect reports}}.
column2:
The starting row includes the current employee. Each recursive step adds the reports of employees already found. The final set therefore contains the employee, direct reports, and indirect reports.
Review source

column1: Disable a policy with ALTER SECURITY POLICY Security.TenantSecurityPolicy WITH (STATE = {{c1::OFF}});
column2:
STATE = OFF keeps the policy definition but stops its enforcement. Rows previously hidden by that policy can become visible to users who already have table access. Do not disable a production policy merely to inspect more rows.
Review source

column1: Extend an existing policy with ALTER SECURITY POLICY Security.TenantSecurityPolicy {{c1::ADD FILTER PREDICATE}} Security.fn_TenantAccessPredicate(TenantID) ON dbo.Shipments;
column2:
ADD FILTER PREDICATE attaches the existing function to dbo.Shipments. The TenantID argument passes each row's tenant value into the access condition. The policy's other table bindings remain in place.
Review source

column1: Remove Orders' filter binding with ALTER SECURITY POLICY Security.TenantSecurityPolicy {{c1::DROP FILTER PREDICATE}} ON dbo.Orders;
column2:
DROP FILTER PREDICATE removes the filter attachment for dbo.Orders. It does not drop the predicate function or the entire policy. Removing the binding removes that filter's protection from Orders.
Review source

column1: Inspect RLS policies and their is_enabled state through {{c1::sys.security_policies}}.
column2:
sys.security_policies has one row per security policy. is_enabled shows whether the policy currently enforces its predicates. A policy can exist in the database while its state is disabled.
Review source

column1: Inspect predicate definitions and target_object_id through {{c1::sys.security_predicates}}.
column2:
sys.security_predicates describes the function bindings within policies. target_object_id identifies the protected table, while object_id identifies the containing policy. These IDs let you connect policy details to table metadata.
Review source

column1: Enabled RLS on a base table also applies through {{c1::views and stored procedures}} that query it.
column2:
A view or stored procedure is another route to the same protected table. The table policy still evaluates the query's effective execution context. A procedure that changes execution context can therefore change which access condition applies.
Review source

column1: An enabled SQL Server RLS policy does not automatically exempt {{c1::dbo}}.
column2:
dbo queries still pass through the enabled policy unless its own condition permits them. However, dbo has authority to change or remove the policy. RLS is not a barrier against an administrator who can change its rules.
Review source

column1: Reading an RLS-protected table still requires {{c1::SELECT}} permission on the requested data.
column2:
SELECT authorizes reading the table or requested columns. RLS then limits which rows that read can return. A predicate that permits a row does not supply missing SELECT permission.
Review source
